                                   PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT       §                          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561 §                                         OF TEXAS


             SKYBOX DATACENTERS COMMENTS TO PROPOSED RULE

                                       I. INTRODUCTION

    Skybox Datacenters, LLC (“Skybox”) appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments
to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“PUCT”) regarding the rulemaking for Large Load
Interconnection Standards under PURA §37.0561. Skybox believes that the PUCT has put
extensive thought and effort into this draft rule and believes that many of the larger concepts
make sense. Skybox has provided a brief summary of our firm below and has produced
comments for the PUCT’s consideration.

   Since 2014, Skybox has been a committed partner in the Texas power region, successfully
commissioning approximately 200 MW of data center capacity in partnership with Oncor and
AEP. Our current momentum reflects a deep investment in the state’s digital infrastructure:

   •   Current Development: 960 MW of ERCOT-approved projects currently under
       development in the Austin and Dallas regions.
   •   Near-Term Delivery: Phased energization scheduled between 2026 and 2030.
   •   Financial Stability: 100% of current developments are leased to investment-grade
       customers, ensuring long-term project viability and predictable load growth.

    Skybox continues to scale its footprint in Texas with several new interconnection agreements
currently in place or in negotiation. Skybox’s goal is to ensure that this growth remains a
strategic asset to the ERCOT grid rather than a liability and is committed to working closely with
the Transmission Service Providers (“TSPs”), ERCOT and the PUCT to ensure high reliability
standards as these projects are delivered.

       Skybox remains a transparent, data-driven partner to the PUCT and ERCOT. We
advocate for standards that balance the need for expedited interconnection with the prudent
planning required to protect the ERCOT system. To that end, Skybox respectfully submits the
following responses to Staff’s questions regarding the proposed rule changes in Project No.
58481.

                                   II. GENERAL COMMENTS

       Skybox recognizes that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing
presents unique structural challenges for energy generators, transmission service providers, and
regulators. We view this transition as a critical juncture for Texas to solidify its position as a



                                                                                                 1
 global leader in technological infrastructure.

       Effectively managing this "Large Load" influx is not merely an economic necessity but a
matter of national security and technological sovereignty. Skybox believes that through
transparent coordination and clear regulatory frameworks, Texas can accommodate this demand
while maintaining the highest standards of grid reliability and consumer affordability.

In order to improve the process Skybox supports and/or suggests:

   •   Prioritizing Performance Metrics in combination with financial securitization of projects
       in order to vet large load interconnection requests across customers through a transparent
       set of metrics and milestones. These are outlined further below in Staff Question #2.
   •   Define large loads by a total peak demand of 75 MW or greater.
   •   Structured financial securitization of projects that allows for deposits to be made to TSPs
       at the beginning of a large load request and for that securitization to be drawn down on
       throughout the process until actual projected costs for the project are known, and then
       implemented into the overall project financial securitization. It is important that the
       financial steps are aligned with milestones towards certainty of interconnection and
       clarity around the amount of load and timing of load delivery. Said simply, as large load
       customers receive more clarity around the timing, sizing and costs of a large load
       interconnection, the financial commitments should scale in step (but recognizing that
       there should be a significant upfront securitization, which Skybox suggest should be
       $20,000 per MW).
   •   Improved transparency in the large load interconnection process between customers, the
       TSPs and ERCOT. Milestones and response times need to be clear.

Strategic Alignment:
   • Skybox is generally aligned with the comments submitted under Project Number 58317
       on December 18, 2025 by Google and Lancium LLC. Their proposed Transmission
       Capacity Planning and Commitment Framework (TCPCF) is highly logical and creates
       many of the steps that Skybox believe would help to make the entire large load
       interconnection process more manageable and the resulting impact economically
       successful while improving system reliability.

   •   Skybox is also generally aligned with the comments submitted under Project Number
       58481 on December 18, 2025 by Google and Lancium LLC.

                    III. RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF QUESTIONS

   1. Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
      customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how
      should the commission define those parameters?

       Skybox aligns with the Data Center Coalition’s (“DCC”) position on this question.




                                                                                                 2
    2. Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
      information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and
      allows a large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should
      the commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not
      competitively sensitive information)? If so, what information should and should
      not be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and
      ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely
      to materialize?

      Skybox believes that while ERCOT Protocol 3.2.7 (listed below) provides a foundation
      for identifying duplicate requests, the Commission should prioritize project maturity
      over simple de-duplication. In the current market, an investment-grade developer may
      submit multiple requests; however, if the customer is qualified and the power is
      available, these often result in multiple viable projects rather than a single "duplicate."

      To help the Commission and ERCOT distinguish between "phantom load" and certain-
      to-be-built infrastructure, Skybox recommends the following:
          • Define Sensitivity by Exception: The Commission should establish a "Safe
             Harbor" list of non-sensitive information required for grid planning—such as
             Load Zone, interconnecting substation, and requested energization date. This
             allows for transparency without compromising a customer’s competitive
             position.

          •   Prioritize Performance Metrics: Rather than attempting to guess a project's
              intent through anonymized data, the Commission should focus on objective
              readiness milestones to validate the queue, including:
                  o The customer’s documented history of performance within ERCOT and
                      other U.S. markets.
                  o The financial securitization provided to the underlying TSP per project
                      submitted to ERCOT.
                  o The maturity of the project site (e.g., site control and permitting status).
                  o The TSP’s fact based opinion of the customer’s ability to perform
                  o The underlying engineering studies, interconnection agreements and
                      design performed to date with the TSP to validate the maturity of the
                      project.

      Skybox supports the disclosure of basic geographic and load data to prevent queue-
      clogging but urges the Commission to use customer performance metrics and project
      maturity as the primary filters for identifying load that is likely to materialize.

Protocol 3.2.7 Language:




                                                                                                    3
 (2) ERCOT must publish a Large Load Interconnection status report each month to the ERCOT

website that aggregates Large Load Interconnection requests across multiple dimensions with as

much specificity as possible while maintaining the confidentiality of Customer data, including:


       (a) Load Zone;


       (b) TSP;


       (c) Load type (as provided to the TSP, such as refinery, steel mill, data center, etc...);


       (d) Calendar quarter and year in which the interconnecting TSP submitted the project to

       ERCOT;


       (e) Requested energization quarter and year;


       (f) Size range;


       (g) Interconnection status (as defined by ERCOT to differentiate between operational,

       approved, under study, etc.); and


       (h) Co-location status.


(3) ERCOT shall take actions such as providing ranges of interconnection MW sizes, aggregate

loads, and other similar actions to protect, anonymize, and otherwise safeguard confidential and

competitively-sensitive Customer data from public disclosure. When aggregating Customer data,

ERCOT should ensure that at least five Customers exist in a particular Load type subcategory prior

to aggregation, to protect against accidental disclosure. ERCOT may leave a certain category blank

or aggregated with other Load types to avoid disclosure.




                                                                                                    4
 3. Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting
   electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed
   in response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If
   only material changes, how should "material change" be defined?

   Skybox believes that material changes should only include modifications pertaining to
   interconnection such as location, MW size, load ramp, delivery date, and backup
   generation capacity. Information unrelated to securing and delivering energy would
   create unnecessary compliance workload without improving reliability.

4. Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund
   20% of a large load customer' s security after energization and ratably as the large
   load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer' s schedule for
   phased energization of its contracted load. Should the commission standardize the
   rate for refund for reaching milestones identified in the customer's schedule for
   phased energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations until the full amount of
   security is refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?

   Skybox agrees with the DCC’s position in their comments on 58481 as posted on
   12/19/2025, encouraging that the Commission structure rule language to align with
   milestones rather than time lapsed. Milestones ensure that the agreements are focused
   on completing projects. If projects are not moving forward, time is not the best
   measurement.

5. Are changes to the commission' s other substantive rules necessary to align with
   this rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?

   Skybox has provided changes below to the Large Load Interconnection (“LLI”)
   process, but requests consideration of the following condition:

   If a large load customer has an existing executed discretionary service agreement or
   interconnection agreement with an interconnecting electric utility and the large load
   customer has securitized at least $10,000,000 with the interconnecting electric utility,
   these new Large Load Interconnection provisions shall not apply.

   Skybox would suggest that the current approach is insufficient to manage the current
   volume of Large Load Interconnection (LLI) requests. We propose a more formalized
   Three-Phase Readiness Framework designed to filter speculative requests and prioritize
   projects with the highest probability of energization.

   •   Phase I: TDSP Validation and "Project Maturity Rating"
          o Before an LLI request is elevated to ERCOT, the Transmission and
              Distribution Service Provider (TDSP) must verify a project’s viability.
              Skybox proposes a Project Maturity Rating based on the following criteria:
                 § Technical Readiness: Submission of completed dynamic load models,
                     load ramp projections, and preliminary engineering studies.


                                                                                              5
                   §   Financial Commitment:
                          • Payment of non-refundable engineering study fees (in line with
                             the proposed $150k–$300k range).
                          • Security Deposit: A refundable or applicable to later costs
                             "Queue Position Deposit" of $20,000 per MW to demonstrate
                             project capitalization.
                  §   Verified documentation of Site Control and execution of a
                      Discretionary Services Agreement (DSA).
                  §   Customer Track Record: Evidence of the customer’s historical
                      performance and reliability within ERCOT or other major ISOs.

   •   Phase II: ERCOT Expedited Review and Queue Securitization
       Upon receipt of a validated PMR from the TDSP, the project enters the ERCOT
       review cycle:
           o System Impact Review: ERCOT completes its study within a 30–60 day
              window.
           o Conditional Approval: Once the study is returned, the developer is granted a
              60-day "Securitization Window."
           o Final Activation: During this window, the developer must execute a formal
              Interconnection Agreement (IA) and post any necessary Contributions in Aid
              of Construction (CIAC).
                  § Note: To avoid capital inefficiency, the initial $20,000/MW deposit
                     should be credited toward the final security requirements or CIAC, but
                     should not be a cap and the CIAC and financial security should be
                     adequate to cover TDSP’s downside risks.

   •   Phase III: Queue Discipline and Performance Requirements
       To maintain rigor in the queue Skybox proposes the following provisions:

          o Forfeiture of Position: Failure to execute an IA or satisfy financial security
            requirements within the 60-day window results in an immediate loss of queue
            position.
          o Restudy Requirement: Any project failing to meet Phase II milestones must
            re-enter the process as a new request, requiring an updated System Impact
            Study to reflect current grid conditions.

                 IV. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR RULE PROPOSAL

Skybox supports the Data Center Coalition’s comments on this section per their most
recent (12/19/25) submission on Project 58481.

Dallas, TX 75219

                SKYBOX DATACENTERS LLC EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Skybox Datacenters, LLC is a committed partner in the Texas power region with approximately
200 MW of commissioned capacity and 960 MW of ERCOT-approved projects currently under
development. Skybox views the management of "Large Load" influx as a critical juncture for
Texas to maintain grid reliability and technological sovereignty. Below is a summary of
Skybox’s position and recommendations:

   •   Definition of Large Load: Skybox recommends defining large loads by a total peak
       demand of 75 MW or greater.

   •   Three-Phase Readiness Framework: Skybox proposes a formalized framework to filter
       speculative requests, utilizing a "Project Maturity Rating" (PMR) to verify technical
       readiness and financial commitment before moving to ERCOT review.

   •   Financial Securitization: To demonstrate project capitalization and discourage
       "phantom load," Skybox suggests a significant upfront security deposit of $20,000 per
       MW.

   •   Performance-Based Milestones: Rather than time-lapsed refunds, Skybox advocates for
       structured financial securitization that scales with milestones and allows for ratable
       refunds based on project completion and energization.

   •   Project Maturity vs. De-duplication: Skybox urges the Commission to prioritize
       project maturity—such as site control, permitting, and customer track record—as the
       primary filter for identifying viable projects rather than simple de-duplication.

   •   Safe Harbor Disclosures: Skybox supports establishing a "Safe Harbor" list of non-
       sensitive information (e.g., Load Zone and requested energization date) to improve
       transparency while protecting competitively sensitive data.

   •   Queue Discipline: To maintain queue rigor, Skybox proposes that failure to execute an
       Interconnection Agreement or satisfy financial requirements within a 60-day window
       should result in immediate loss of queue position.

   •   Grandfathering Provision: Skybox requests that new LLI provisions not apply to
       customers with existing executed agreements who have already securitized at least
       $10,000,000 with their interconnecting utility.

   •   Strategic Alignment: Skybox generally aligns with the Transmission Capacity Planning
       and Commitment Framework (TCPCF) proposed by Google and Lancium LLC in their
       12/18/2025 filing on Project Number 58317, as well as their positions in their 12/18/25
       filing on Project Number 58481, and Skybox is also generally aligned with the positions
       of the Data Center Coalition (DCC) in their 12/19/2025 filing on Project Number 58481.
